Conversation 1, Welcome to Business Matters.
Today we have invited career development consultant Lucy Williams to talk about how to
get a head at work.
Hi Lucy.
Many of us never seem to get promoted.
Why is that?
And what can we do about it?
When mistake people make is the limit communication only to their bosses.
It's important to expand your network and include your co-workers.
But some of our co-workers are less senior to us.
Is it really necessary to connect with them?
It's important not to underestimate your colleagues.
Sometimes a job title might not clearly demonstrate the influence they may have.
Now many of us think that working hard creates a good impression, but this isn't always
true, is it?
That's right.
We should avoid trying to take on too much work and constantly staying late, just to show
that you are committed.
I see.
So setting expectations too high at the beginning can make us look bad if we don't maintain
them.
Yeah.
It's better to make sure you are putting in quality time, instead of just a large quantity
of time.
And these efforts can easily be demonstrated by the results we achieve.
What about helping others at work?
Did you try and go beyond your normal responsibilities and offer to help people with their
projects?
Extend your assistance to those who need it, but only as long as your own work will not
go unattended.
If someone can benefit from your assistance or advice, help them out to gain their respect
and trust.
But it goes without saying that you shouldn't act like a know-it-all.
Otherwise you'll appear arrogant.
Absolutely.
Be humble.
And you'll get a lot of time later on to show your genius.

Passage one.
Makeup can do more than just change your appearance.
It can also alter others' perceptions of you for better or for worse.
According to new research from the University of Sterling in Scotland, although both men
and women perceive women who wear makeup as being of a higher status, men associate makeup
with prestigious positive qualities, while women view other women wearing makeup as being
dominant and a potential threat.
The research showed that men and women both rated the faces with cosmetics as being more
attractive.
But only women rated made up faces as being more dominant, while only men rated made up
faces as being higher in prestige.
A follow-up study investigated the root cause behind these differences in perception and
found that female on female jealousy seemed to be the main cause for the differences in
perception.
Women rating women with makeup said they would be more jealous of them and thought they
would be more attractive to men than their non-makeup wearing counterparts.
If products are good for more than just giving you a pretty face, it can be particularly
useful for women to understand how wearing makeup alters others' perceptions of them in situations
where they are trying to gain others' trust and admiration.
At a job interview, knowing whether the hiring committee will consist of men or women might
influence a female candidate's decision about wearing makeup.
Whether the interviewers will view her as attractive, dominant, and prestigious can affect
the interviewer's actions and perhaps the outcome of the interview itself.

Passage 2.
You may have seen advertisements trumpeting methods of changing a habit that require absolutely
no willpower whatsoever, but can you really change a bad habit or create a good one without
willpower?
To answer this question, we first have to ask, what is willpower?
Most people sadly think of it only as the ability to clench their teeth and resist
attractive temptations.
In this view, willpower means self-denial and no fun.
No one that people hope to make changes without it.
I define willpower as using only the thought of your motivators to control your actions.
Let's say your motivators are prevent diabetes and reach a healthy weight.
So if you are at the all you can eat buffet, you think about your motivator, avoid diabetes
through weight loss, and you take small portions and avoid the dessert table.
So amazingly enough, willpower begins with a thought, a bright idea, some way to improve
your life or contributes to others.
This bright idea is your motivator.
Dr. Walter Mitchell, an expert on willpower skills, uses the expressive term, a burning
goal.
Whether you call it a motivator, a burning goal, or a bright idea, this idea is the force
behind your willpower.
What sort of bright ideas motivators make for effective willpower?
In fact, any goal that you value strongly counts.
The list may include good health, self-respect, a better future for your family, personal
mission, and being a role model for your child.
All these can certainly drive a positive change.

Question 14.
For many pregnant women, understanding what seafood is safe and healthy and what should
be avoided because of mercury concerns comes with a lot of worrying.
In part, that's because the federal government's advice on the matter, first issued
in 2004, has long been criticized as vague.
But guidance has included advice on how much seafood to eat, and which species pregnant
and breastfeeding women should avoid over concerns about mercury contamination.
But critics say the government advisory has done more harm than good, scaring many pregnant
and breastfeeding women away from eating seafood altogether.
The problem is real.
According to a spokesman for the Food and Drug Administration or FDA for short, the
agency analyzed fish consumption data from more than 1,000 pregnant women in the US,
and found that 21% of them ate no fish whatsoever in the previous month.
And those who did eat fish consumed far less than recommended by the dietary guidelines.
Some 50%, ate less than two ounces a week, and 75%, ate less than four ounces.
This week, the FDA issued an update to the advice, listing more than 60 species in a chart
that ranks fish as a best choice, good choice, and choices to avoid.
The goal is to make it easier for mothers to be to feel confident about the type of seafood
they include in their diets.
The new advice recommends consumers choose a variety of fish to eat, and it comes with
an easy-to-understand illustration of what an appropriate portion size should be.
Four ounces for an adult, and two ounces for children aged four to seven.
And while expected mothers have long been warned to stay away from shark and for other
particular types of fish from the Gulf of Mexico, now there are three new species on
the list of what to avoid.
But not everyone is thrilled with the new advice.
The new advice doesn't always agree with the agency's own scientific findings.
While mercury is of great concern when people are talking about pregnant women and seafood,
it's not the only factor contributing to anxiety.
The FDA maintains that its final consumption recommendations were based on thorough scientific
analysis.
Lucy Spokesman Cassell says the FDA believes the recommendations will increase confidence,
not uncertainty.
But critics disagree.
They think the FDA's advice is not based on the evidence in its own detailed report,
and so it confuses everyone.

I know you're busy with work, but you also need to take some time off to recharge
those batteries.
So should you plan one big vacation for the year or should you take multiple short vacations
throughout?
Quantity can sometimes beat quality.
First and foremost, regardless of how you use your vacation days, you need to be using
them and soon.
The longer you put off your time off, the worse you're making things for yourself.
One nine year long study published in psychosomatic medicine suggests not taking at least
one vacation a year may increase your risk of mortality due to heart disease.
So not only are you killing your joy, you're possibly killing yourself.
Give yourself a break, folks.
When you should take those breaks, however, depends on a few factors.
How many days you have available to use?
What activities bring you joy?
Whether you have a family or not and other variables come into play.
Because of that, there's no perfect formula that works for everyone.
But there are still a few things everyone can try to shoot for.
We know that in terms of maximizing relaxation, you should aim for vacations that range somewhere
between seven and 11 days long.
That gives you enough time to let go of your stress at work, completely loosen up, and
achieve full-on calm.
That above mentioned study also recommends you space out your vacations evenly instead
of using up all of your days at once.
Eight days might sound like a lot for someone who only gets 10 days of vacation a year.
But if you frame them with weekends, you can manage two evenly spaced eight day vacations
a year.
If you have 14 days of paid leave, that's almost three separate eight day vacations you
can use to split your year into thirds.
As tempting as it might be to use all your days to take one long summer break, your
overall goal should be to achieve the perfect balance between length plus joy and frequency.
Vacation frequency is important because planning multiple breaks throughout the year means
you always have something to look forward to.
Planning things and the anticipation that comes with it tends to make us happier.
If you only take one long vacation every year, the excitement builds much more slowly and
seems so far off that it can actually lead to feelings of despair.

Question 23, autonomous cars that can take over from drivers if they are tired or caught
in the heat of an argument are being developed in Sweden.
Researchers working as part of the European Union's 77 billion euro research program are developing
sensor based systems that monitor whether a driver is distracted, anxious or tired.
If a driver is not in a fit state to be on the road, the car automatically takes control
of the wheel to prevent accidents.
Dr. Anna Anund from the Swedish National Road and Transport Research Institute who is leading
the project said a driver's state can be measured using a number of sensors including heart
rate monitors and eye sensors which track where a driver's gaze is.
She said the aim was to really make sure that the transition from the driver to the vehicle
is done in a safe way.
So we can take into consideration the driver's state and so we do not give control to
a driver who is under pressure of fatigue, stress, anxiety and so on.
According to data from the European Commission, Sweden has the safest roads in the EU with
the UK a close second.
However, the number of road accidents in both has largely leveled out since 2010.
However, fatigue is thought to be responsible for as many as a fifth of road crashes
across the EU, although there are certain times of the day when more accidents happen.
At 6am for example, drivers are said to be 20 times more likely to have an accident than
at 10am.
While most experts agree driverless technology should help bring down accident numbers in
the long term, some have questioned whether it is safe.
The researchers have said the technology they are developing is seeking to bridge the gap
between level 3 on the autonomy scale in which drivers have to be ready to take control
of the car at any point and level 4 in which driving is automated.
Daniel Ruiz, the chief executive of the UK's connected and autonomous vehicle program
Meridian, said there is a strong debate going on about how it is possible to make
a level 3 car completely safe.
Despite advances in technology, we still have some way to go in shifting public sentiment.
With an increase in attention grabbing accidents recently, drivers now view self-driving
cars as less safe than they used to.
